ut_donnelly_canyon.blurb: Donnelly Canyon is a short side canyon at Indian Creek, lined with sandstone crack climbs that are almost entirely trad. Most of the lines fall between 5.10 and 5.12, with a handful of easier ones and a single bolted line, so it suits climbers who are comfortable jamming and placing gear. The easier cracks make it busy, and the parking area and trail get plenty of traffic. The walls start right at the trail, so there is no long approach. Desert sandstone is fragile when wet, so wait out rain before climbing.

ut_5_mile_boulders.blurb: Five Mile is one of the best-loved bouldering areas in Little Cottonwood Canyon, found roughly five miles up the road on the north side. The granite offers a bit of everything: cracks, aretes, technical slopers with mantles, and a sprinkling of hard problems up to the V10 range. Most of the problems sit in the V4 to V6 zone, with a good number of easier ones too. Because it is low in the canyon and faces the sun, it can stay dry when higher areas hold snow, which makes it a useful winter option. Pads and spotters are a must, and parking room is tight on busy days.

ut_membrane_the.blurb: The Membrane is a north-facing limestone sport crag in American Fork Canyon, and one of the most popular walls in the canyon. Its routes run from about 5.9 to 5.13, with most between 5.10 and 5.12, on jug-heavy rock that is steep and fun. Bolts are not close together everywhere, so expect some spaced clips. The wall stays shaded nearly all day, which makes it a good escape when it is hot elsewhere, and the walk from the road is just a couple of minutes. It often has climbers on it, so a weekend can mean a short wait.

ut_1st_meat_wall.blurb: First Meat is a steep sandstone wall in the Indian Creek corridor, all trad crack climbing. About two thirds of the lines are 5.10, with a smaller number of 5.11 and 5.12 cracks and only a couple of easier ones. Of the three Meat Walls it sees the least traffic, so it can be a quieter pick than its neighbors. The reward comes with some effort: the trail up is faint and steep, and the dirt road in can be rough. Bring a standard Creek rack with plenty of the sizes you plan to repeat.

ut_wailing_wall_the.blurb: The Wailing Wall is a big, steep limestone face at Welcome Springs, just around the corner from the Cathedral, in the desert west of St. George. The wall faces north and the climbing is all sport, mostly vertical to slightly overhanging and quite hard: nearly all of it is 5.11 and up, with the bulk in the 5.12 range and a few 5.13s and beyond. Getting there takes a real walk in along a stream and a fixed line to reach ledges below the cliff, so it is a committed day out for strong sport climbers rather than a casual stop.

ut_shattered_sea.blurb: Shattered Sea is a sport crag on the Aquarius Plateau, at over 10,000 feet in the Jungle area. The volcanic rock is welded tuff, solid in places and grainy in others, and the routes are short enough that a 40 meter rope is plenty. Grades sit in a friendly range, mostly 5.9 to 5.11 with a few easier lines, and the wall stays in shade until late afternoon, which helps on hot days. Expect a rough high-clearance road and a cairned walk through some deadfall to get in. Afternoon thunderstorms are common in midsummer, and fall is a pleasant time to visit.
